lessons.title: Define the service before choosing a GPU
lessons.summary: An interactive chat, an overnight batch job and an embedding endpoint need different serving contracts.

concepts.detail: Record prompt/output length distributions, arrival bursts, concurrency, languages and privacy needs.
Interactive serving optimizes waiting and streaming; offline jobs prioritize completion windows and throughput.
A service-level objective describes a user outcome over a stated window. Availability, latency and answer quality are separate.

lessons.signals: Measure request mix, admission failures and first-output/whole-response latency by bounded workload class.
lessons.pitfall: Fast tokens are not useful if the answer is wrong or most visitors are rejected.
lessons.exercise: Write a one-page contract: audience, model task, context/output limits, latency targets, quality gate and monthly spending ceiling.

quiz.question: Does a high tokens/sec result prove a good chat experience?
choices: No: latency, errors and quality also matter.
Yes, throughput is the only user metric.
quiz.explanation: Throughput is a system metric. Define the user-visible outcome and its denominator before optimizing.

lessons.title: Ship a model as a versioned artifact
lessons.summary: A model is more than a weight file: reproducibility depends on everything that interprets it.

concepts.detail: Compare task quality, license, context support and the runtime's supported model architecture.
Pin weight checksum, tokenizer, chat template, model configuration, quantization format and engine/container version.
Download, read, load, compile or capture kernels, warm up, then pass readiness before receiving traffic.

lessons.signals: Track load/warm-up time, artifact failures, ready replicas and deployed model/engine versions.
lessons.pitfall: A compatible HTTP API does not guarantee the same tokenizer, sampling, usage fields or model quality.
lessons.exercise: Inspect the repository's pinned model downloader and CPU profile. Record their checksums and explain a safe rollback.

quiz.question: What belongs with the weights in a reproducible release?
choices: Tokenizer, template, configuration and engine version.
quiz.explanation: The same bytes can behave differently under a different template, tokenizer or runtime.

lessons.title: Tokens, context and generation controls
lessons.summary: The model sees token IDs, not words. The serialized conversation must fit its context budget.

concepts.detail: Roles, system instructions, tools and retrieved text consume input tokens. A token is not a word or necessarily one streamed chunk.
Temperature changes probability sharpness; top-k/top-p restrict candidates. Stop sequences, EOS and output caps determine termination.
Cached tokens are part of input; reported reasoning tokens are part of output. Unsupported details stay unknown. Extended tokens is not a universal field.

lessons.signals: Track input/output distributions, context-limit errors, stop reasons and missing-usage rate without logging hidden reasoning.
lessons.pitfall: Adding cached input or reasoning a second time inflates total usage; visible words cannot reconstruct true token counts.
lessons.exercise: Use the token ledger below. Then compare two chat templates locally and count the serialized prompt with the actual tokenizer.

quiz.question: Input 1,000 (400 cached), output 200 (50 reasoning): total?
quiz.explanation: Total is input + output. Both cached input and reasoning are overlapping subsets.

lessons.title: Prefill, decode and the streaming boundary
lessons.summary: Follow one request through the gateway, queue, model and network before drawing a latency conclusion.

concepts.detail: Process the input and build attention state. The final prompt position can already provide logits for the first generated token.
Generate subsequent tokens using cached state. Prefill is often compute-heavy; small-batch decode is often bandwidth-sensitive, not universally so.
TTFT stops at first visible content. TPOT is an average over output intervals; ITL measures individual token gaps only when token boundaries are known.

lessons.signals: Capture client and server clocks separately, queue/prefill durations, stream gaps, cancellations and end-to-end completion.
lessons.pitfall: Do not sum nested spans, subtract timestamps from different machines or equate an SSE chunk to one token.
lessons.exercise: Play the homepage tour, then use the latency budget below to distinguish queue delay from KV-transfer delay.

quiz.question: A proxy buffers the response. Which latency can worsen without slower model execution?
quiz.explanation: Client TTFT includes transport and buffering outside the engine's timing boundary.

lessons.title: CPU, GPU and the full memory budget
lessons.summary: Capacity asks whether it fits; bandwidth asks how quickly bytes move; compute asks how fast the math runs.

concepts.detail: CPU cores use caches and host DRAM. GPU compute uses on-chip storage plus device memory such as HBM or GDDR. PCIe/NVLink are links, not memory capacity.
Budget weights, active KV, temporary activations/workspace and runtime overhead. Quantized weights do not imply quantized KV.
MHA, GQA and MQA have different KV-head counts. MLA, sliding windows and hybrid state-space models need different accounting.

lessons.signals: Observe process RSS/cgroups and CPU throttling; on GPU hosts add device memory, compute activity, bandwidth, power and thermal throttling.
lessons.pitfall: A1 has CPU and host RAM, not a GPU or HBM. A theoretical memory bound is not utilization or achieved tokens/sec.
lessons.exercise: Change context and concurrent sequences in the memory calculator. Explain why KV grows while weight memory stays fixed.

quiz.question: Halving weight precision necessarily halves KV memory?
quiz.explanation: Weights and KV have separate formats. The calculation also needs attention architecture and sequence lengths.

lessons.title: Admission, continuous batching and fairness
lessons.summary: The scheduler decides who waits and which requests share the next execution step.

concepts.detail: Bound running work, queued work, input length and output reservation. Reject overload early instead of building an unbounded queue.
An engine can retire finished sequences and admit new ones between iterations, unlike a fixed batch that waits for its slowest member.
Split long prompt work into smaller scheduling units to reduce interference with ongoing decode; tune against both TTFT and token-gap targets.

lessons.signals: Watch queue age/depth, active sequences, scheduled tokens per step, preemptions and tenant fairness.
lessons.pitfall: A bigger batch can increase throughput and worsen latency. CPU usage alone does not explain scheduler pressure.
lessons.exercise: Use the traffic exercise below to see bounded admission. For real continuous batching, compare an engine with equal hardware and a fixed workload.

quiz.question: Why split a long prefill into chunks?
choices: To guarantee lower latency for every request.
To limit how long prompt work interferes with other work.
quiz.explanation: Chunking is a scheduling tradeoff. It is not an unconditional speedup.

lessons.title: Paged KV, prefix reuse and cache eviction
lessons.summary: Cache mechanisms reuse different things. Keep their keys, lifetimes and correctness rules distinct.

concepts.detail: Allocate token state in blocks and map logical sequence positions to physical storage. This reduces waste; it is not disk paging by definition.
Reuse compatible state for an identical prefix. A warm prefix can reduce prefill work but does not eliminate generation for a new answer.
A response cache reuses answers and needs freshness/tenant rules. KV offload moves state to another memory tier and trades capacity for transfer cost.

lessons.signals: Measure prefix hit tokens, misses, evictions, allocated/free blocks, recomputation and offload bytes/latency.
lessons.pitfall: Cache keys must account for model, adapter, tokenization and isolation. Semantic similarity alone cannot establish identical KV state.
lessons.exercise: Compare cold and warm prefixes locally. Change the model or adapter and explain why blindly reusing state would be unsafe.

quiz.question: Does PagedAttention mean KV is always stored on disk?
choices: No; it is a block-based memory-management approach.
Yes; every token uses object storage.
quiz.explanation: Paging describes logical-to-physical block mapping; offload is a separate capability.

lessons.title: Kernels, quantization and speculative decoding
lessons.summary: Optimize the bottleneck you measured, then retest quality and workload-wide performance.

concepts.detail: Fusion and graph capture can reduce launch overhead. FlashAttention reduces attention-related memory traffic through tiling; it is not prefix caching.
Lower-precision weights or KV can reduce memory. Kernel support, metadata and accuracy determine the real benefit.
A draft proposes tokens and a target verifies them. Exact methods preserve the target distribution under their assumptions; draft cost and acceptance determine speedup.

lessons.signals: Profile kernel time and memory traffic; report speculative acceptance, draft/verify cost, decode latency and quality regressions.
lessons.pitfall: Do not quote a paper's speedup as your benchmark. A draft model adds memory and may make an unsuitable workload slower.
lessons.exercise: List the baseline, one optimization, equal resource budget and quality gate. Treat the public calculators as hypotheses, not a kernel benchmark.

quiz.question: What does low draft acceptance tend to do?
choices: Waste more proposal work and reduce potential speedup.
Remove the need for the target model.
quiz.explanation: Rejected proposals still cost work. Measure net end-to-end performance, not just acceptance.

lessons.title: Replicas, sharding and GPU topology
lessons.summary: More devices can add replicas or split one model. These are different scaling strategies.

concepts.detail: Data parallelism replicates serving capacity; tensor parallelism splits layer math; pipeline parallelism assigns different layers or stages to devices.
Expert parallelism distributes MoE experts; context parallelism splits long-sequence work. Communication patterns differ.
Collectives such as all-reduce/all-to-all depend on PCIe, NVLink, NIC placement and inter-node networking. NUMA locality also matters on CPU hosts.

lessons.signals: Measure collective time, link bandwidth, imbalance, per-rank memory and tokens/sec per device.
lessons.pitfall: Two GPUs do not automatically double speed. A model split across ranks can fail when one rank or link fails.
lessons.exercise: Draw one replicated model versus one tensor-sharded model. Identify which can survive losing one instance without rebuilding a distributed group.

quiz.question: Which choice splits a layer's computation across devices?
quiz.explanation: Tensor parallelism shards within model computation and introduces synchronization.

lessons.title: Separate prefill and decode deliberately
lessons.summary: Disaggregated serving gives each phase its own capacity pool, but makes the cache handoff a distributed-system problem.

concepts.detail: Tune prefill and decode capacity independently and reduce interference between their workload shapes.
Move compatible attention state, plus ownership/position metadata, to the selected decode worker. Serialization, setup and link contention add cost.
Track destination readiness, cache lifecycle, retries and failed/partial transfers. RDMA or NIXL support is engine- and deployment-specific.

lessons.signals: Observe prefill/decode queue imbalance, transfer size/time/failure, cache residency and goodput under both latency targets.
lessons.pitfall: Disaggregation is not always faster. Compare against a combined baseline using the same total hardware budget.
lessons.exercise: Move the bandwidth slider below. The repository lab models a handoff; only a real compatible multi-worker engine can prove tensor transport.

quiz.question: When can disaggregation be worse?
choices: When handoff and coordination costs outweigh separation benefits.
Only when output has zero words.
quiz.explanation: Placement, workload and link behavior determine whether separation is worth its cost.

lessons.title: From a laptop to an OCI or GPU cluster
lessons.summary: Understand the infrastructure beneath the model before adding an orchestrator.

concepts.detail: Choose CPU/GPU shape, RAM/device memory, model storage, image registry and driver/runtime compatibility. Cache model downloads and budget startup I/O.
Use VCN/subnets, routes, NSGs/firewall rules, DNS, TLS and least-privilege IAM. Keep model and operator endpoints private.
Containers isolate processes; Kubernetes adds scheduling, resource requests/limits, GPU device plugins, placement and health management. It is optional for one VM.

lessons.signals: Monitor node health, disk space/I/O, network failures, CPU quotas, ready capacity, failed scheduling and regional quota/capacity errors.
lessons.pitfall: Free Tier eligibility is not a guarantee of available capacity. Do not provision a paid GPU or managed cluster implicitly.
lessons.exercise: Trace internet → HTTPS → private gateway/model on the Phoenix diagram. Mark every port, trust boundary and storage volume before applying Terraform.

quiz.question: Does learning Kubernetes require deploying it on your A1 VM now?
choices: No; learn the design while running the one-VM profile.
Only if the model is quantized.
quiz.explanation: Use infrastructure proportional to the workload. The current OCI blueprint remains one CPU VM.

lessons.title: Routing, readiness and autoscaling
lessons.summary: A running process is not necessarily ready to answer. A new replica is not immediately useful capacity.

concepts.detail: Balance queue pressure and locality. Cache-aware routing may improve reuse but can overload a popular replica; tenancy and fairness still apply.
Startup probes allow loading time, readiness gates traffic, and liveness detects a stuck process. A normal long request is not automatically a liveness failure.
Combine arrival load, queued tokens, active sequences and latency with measured capacity. Account for warm-up, cooldown, scale-to-zero delay and stream draining.

lessons.signals: Compare desired/ready replicas, oldest queue age, cold starts, load imbalance and scale-down cancellations.
lessons.pitfall: Autoscaling cannot fix exhausted regional capacity or an unavailable model artifact; CPU-only triggers may miss GPU bottlenecks.
lessons.exercise: Write a scale-out trigger and a safe scale-in procedure. Explain why removing a worker halfway through a stream is risky.

quiz.question: Which probe should stop traffic to a model that is still loading?
choices: Readiness, with startup protection for loading.
quiz.explanation: Readiness controls traffic eligibility; startup checks prevent premature liveness restarts.

lessons.title: Metrics, traces, logs and profiling
lessons.summary: Use signals from every layer, and keep evidence types and clocks explicit.

concepts.detail: Use latency histograms, error/admission counters, token rates, queue gauges and memory signals. Bound labels; request IDs and prompt text do not belong in metric labels.
Propagate trace context through gateway, retrieval and engine boundaries. Redact content and secrets; sample with an explicit policy. One trace can explain what aggregate charts cannot.
Profiles explain CPU/kernel hotspots. Tag results as measured, reported, simulated or analytical; record exporter and semantic-convention versions.

lessons.signals: Start with user outcome → admission/queue → model → hardware → dependency. Monitor telemetry loss and the monitoring system itself.
lessons.pitfall: Missing GPU or reasoning fields are unknown, not zero. Gateway duration does not reveal engine-internal prefill without instrumentation.
lessons.exercise: Use the signal map below to choose the first dashboard and trace for a slow request. Then compare the repository's assistant_* and lab_* contracts.

quiz.question: Should a prompt or unique request ID be a Prometheus label?
choices: No; it leaks content and/or creates unbounded cardinality.
Yes, it makes every chart faster.
quiz.explanation: Use redacted, access-controlled traces/logs for per-request detail and bounded metric dimensions for aggregation.

lessons.title: Load tests, percentiles and error budgets
lessons.summary: A benchmark is a controlled experiment, not one impressive screenshot.

concepts.detail: Closed-loop workers slow their arrivals when the service slows. Open-loop arrivals expose queue buildup; record the offered and accepted workload.
Report sample size, warm-up/cache state, p50/p95/p99, errors and successful throughput. Goodput counts requests that meet all defined SLO conditions per wall-clock second.
Define eligible events and the evaluation window. Multiwindow burn-rate alerts distinguish urgent failures from low-rate noise.

lessons.signals: Measure rejected, failed, timed-out, cancelled and SLO-violating requests, not just successful streams.
lessons.pitfall: A small-sample p99 is unstable. Combining different hardware or warm-cache states invalidates a simple speedup claim.
lessons.exercise: Use the traffic exercise, then create a real test matrix: short/long inputs, short/long outputs, burst/steady load, cold/warm cache and repeated runs.

quiz.question: Should failed requests vanish from a latency/availability report?
choices: No; report failures and their denominators explicitly.
quiz.explanation: Successful latency alone can improve while the system rejects more visitors.

lessons.title: Timeouts, overload and recovery
lessons.summary: Design the unhappy path before opening the service to strangers.

concepts.detail: Apply deadlines, cancellation, output caps, queue limits and backpressure. Stop expensive model work when a client disconnects when the engine supports it.
Use bounded retry budgets and jitter. A partially delivered stream or side-effecting tool call cannot be blindly replayed; use idempotency where supported.
Drain requests during rollout, test backup restoration, define RPO/RTO and distinguish one-node recovery from multi-zone high availability.

lessons.signals: Track cancellations, abandoned admissions, retry amplification, OOM/restarts, recovery time and backup/restore outcomes.
lessons.pitfall: Restarting endlessly is not resilience. Circuit breakers and load shedding protect dependencies but need explicit recovery behavior.
lessons.exercise: Tabletop a model crash during streaming. Specify what the user sees, how quota is reconciled and how the operator verifies recovery.

quiz.question: After half an answer is delivered, should the gateway silently retry forever?
choices: Yes, if the model is small.
No; partial output and repeated work need explicit policy.
quiz.explanation: A retry may duplicate content, cost or tool side effects. Bound it and surface the outcome.

lessons.title: Security, privacy and tenant isolation
lessons.summary: Treat public prompts, retrieved documents and model output as untrusted data.

concepts.detail: Use TLS, authentication/authorization, secret rotation, quotas, body/context limits, network isolation and audited administrative actions.
Prompt injection, retrieval poisoning, unsafe output use and excessive tool permissions require controls outside the model.
Enforce tenant access before retrieval/cache reuse. Minimize content collection, define retention/deletion and protect model artifacts and logs.

lessons.signals: Monitor denied access, abuse patterns, quota anomalies and audit events without placing secrets or personal text in telemetry.
lessons.pitfall: A safety instruction is not an authorization boundary. Schema-valid JSON is not safe shell code or a trusted database operation.
lessons.exercise: Threat-model one tenant trying to read another tenant's document/cache. Mark each enforceable access check outside the model.

quiz.question: Can a system prompt replace authorization on a tool?
choices: No; the tool must enforce permissions independently.
quiz.explanation: Models can be manipulated or mistaken. The receiving system must validate identity, scope and inputs.

lessons.title: RAG, structured outputs and tool workflows
lessons.summary: A model call may be only one step in a larger request.

concepts.detail: Ingest, chunk, embed/index, retrieve and optionally rerank authorized material. Context assembly adds tokens and latency; retrieval is not model training.
Constrain and validate the output schema, then validate meaning and allowed values. Parse failures and factual errors are different.
Tool calls add dependency latency, permissions, retries and possible side effects. Bound iteration count, execution time and total token/tool spend.

lessons.signals: Track retrieval latency/recall, empty results, grounded-answer quality, parse failures, tool errors and per-step token/cost totals.
lessons.pitfall: An answer with citation IDs is not necessarily supported by the sources. Retrieved text must not become privileged instructions.
lessons.exercise: Compare the repository's lexical retrieval with a proposed vector pipeline. Write an authorization check and evaluation set before adding uploads/tools.

quiz.question: Does RAG update the model weights for each document?
choices: No; it supplies retrieved context at inference time.
quiz.explanation: Retrieval changes context, not weights. Fine-tuning is a separate lifecycle.

lessons.title: Multimodal, LoRA and mixture-of-experts
lessons.summary: Text-only dense-model assumptions do not cover every serving workload.

concepts.detail: Images/audio/video may require decoding, resizing, feature encoders and separate queues. Their token accounting and TTFT boundary are model/provider-specific.
Adapters specialize a base model without replacing all weights. Loading, caching, routing and isolating adapters introduce additional state.
Only selected experts execute for a token, but inactive experts may still occupy memory. Expert placement and routing imbalance can dominate communication.

lessons.signals: Measure preprocessing/encoder latency, media-size limits, adapter load/cache misses, per-expert imbalance and memory residency.
lessons.pitfall: Active parameter count is not the same as resident weight memory. Text-token estimates do not automatically price images or audio.
lessons.exercise: Draw the extra stages for a screenshot question, then list how its telemetry and limits differ from text-only serving.

quiz.question: An MoE activates a fraction of experts. Can you budget only active weights in memory?
choices: No; resident experts and the deployment strategy determine memory.
quiz.explanation: Execution sparsity and memory residency are different; offload adds its own costs.

lessons.title: Quality gates and safe model releases
lessons.summary: A service can stay fast and available while its answers get worse.

concepts.detail: Use held-out, task-specific cases for correctness, groundedness, safety, structured output and tool success. Human or model judging needs calibration and error analysis.
Version model, tokenizer, template, adapter, corpus, engine and policy together. Quantization or prompt changes are behavior changes.
Compare a limited rollout with a control on quality, latency, errors and cost. Shadow traffic has privacy/cost implications; obtain the right authorization.

lessons.signals: Track quality by workload slice, regression rates, truncation/invalid citations, canary divergence and rollback time.
lessons.pitfall: Passing retrieval fixtures or emitting a valid citation ID is not proof of answer quality. Avoid evaluating only on training examples.
lessons.exercise: Create a release checklist with ten held-out questions, failure examples, latency/cost limits and a tested rollback to a pinned artifact.

quiz.question: What should block a rollout even if latency improves?
choices: A material regression in the agreed quality or safety gate.
A different timestamp on the file.
quiz.explanation: Serving success includes the task outcome, not only a healthy HTTP response.

lessons.title: Cost, capacity and an end-to-end capstone
lessons.summary: Optimize cost per useful outcome, including idle capacity and the work that fails.

concepts.detail: Include compute hours, storage, network/egress, idle warm replicas, monitoring, retries and external model/tool calls. Use actual prices and billing units.
Cost per SLO-compliant completion can rise even when raw tokens/sec improves. Prompt mix, rejection and quality all affect the denominator.
Specify → pin artifacts → secure infrastructure → serve → instrument → load-test → evaluate → release → recover. Save evidence and document limits at every stage.

lessons.signals: Track total spend, allocated versus useful capacity, cost per accepted/SLO-compliant request and budget forecasts. Alerts are not spending caps.
lessons.pitfall: The public site uses no model API and deploys no OCI resources. A hypothetical cost slider is not an OCI price quote or a free guarantee.
lessons.exercise: Deliver a reproducible Phoenix CPU demo: architecture, IaC plan, pinned model, threat model, measured receipts, SLO/quality report, restore drill and cost assumptions. GPU/HA work stays optional.

quiz.question: What is the better cost denominator for an SLO-focused service?
choices: Every token, even from failed work.
Useful completions that meet the defined objective.
quiz.explanation: Include all relevant costs and state which completions qualify. Quality must be evaluated separately.
